utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is no reason to delay it, may the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: General Kovacevic, good morning to you. Before I invite Mr. Cvijetic to continue his cross-examination, I give you the usual reminder about your solemn declaration. Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We're going to continue, and I'm going to show you an exhibit that we saw yesterday but not these particular provisions. So this is L31, exhibit from our law library.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, L33.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it's your tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to wait for the document to appear on our screens. At least there's nothing on my screen. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us just look which particular piece of legislation this is. This is the Law on National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We looked at it yesterday. That's the law dated 28th of February, 1992, which you can see the heading. Can you see the heading?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And let's move immediately to page 2 in the Serbian, and the same page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, could you please just take a look at it to see what it contains.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this particular article, and I relied on it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What I would like to emphasise is that in the process of organising and preparing for the defence, among other powers that the president of the republic has, can order the use of the police unit during wartime and in peacetime and also in some other emergency situations. Now, General, this is consistent with your position and also the position that stems from the principle of singleness of authority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we have here the president discharging the duties of the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, while we are still on this article, let us just elaborate a little. In other words, nobody else in the military hierarchy except the president of the republic cannot order this particular use; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This cannot be the prerogative of the minister of the interior even, to order the police to take part in armed activities?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless the president of the republic delegates some of his powers on him, then that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we said that it was possible for the president to delegate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down and could the speakers please pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to repeat my question because it's not been recorded due to the fastness of my speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So yesterday we discussed and talked about the fact that the president of the republic may delegate this particular power to the commander of the Main Staff, the commander of the Main Staff can delegate it to the corps commander, and the corps commander can delegate it to the brigade commander. Now, you explained to me that these powers can be transferred up to that level. These powers relating to the use of police units and the process of resubordination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If the minister of the interior decides independently, without relying on any order or a request coming from the military structures and military command, to use the police, that would constitute the overstepping of his authorities, and he would encroach on the competencies of military organs and commanding officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before the general answers, it's unclear to me what the question is. If the minister of the interior decides independently without relying on any order or request coming from the military structures, military -- to use the police. To use the police to do what?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I said but obviously it wasn't interpreted to use it in armed activities. Is now question now complete? General, can you give me an answer? In such case, he would be overstepping his authorities and he would encroach on the authorities that he is not entitled to, those of the president and others from the military hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been speaking these last few days about combat activities where only singleness of command and resubordination can exist. And therefore I agree with you. And I would like to underline that that applies only to combat activities as Ms. Korner rightly pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The minister of the interior, within the ministry, may order this kind of use but exclusively by doing so and executing an order of the superior command. He can never do it independently; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move now to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Cvijetic, before you move on. General, the -- I understand perfectly the answers that you have given to the series of questions that Mr. Cvijetic put, but is there such a thing, in practice, as an implied delegation or the -- having regard to the theoretical and formal structures, particularly based in the laws that you have prescribed, did it always have to be formal and specific? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm afraid I haven't quite understood your question. Are you talking about the use of police or about the powers that the minister has? Can you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I'm thinking of the -- the delegation of authority to the minister, and I'm concentrating on the answers that you gave to Mr. Cvijetic's last set of questions. The -- could there be or was there ever a situation in practice where, although there was no specific directive or permission given to the minister to have the police engage in combat activities, within the practice of what was happening at the time, could the minister have -- could it be implied that the minister had any such authority, although no paper trail, as it were, of any such delegation could ever be found. Is that clearer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand your question, Mr. President. It is possible these things happened in practice. But, in my view, it is much less relevant how a certain police unit becomes integrated into army structure. The military theory and the rules and regulations say that once it becomes part of the military structure, which means as part of combat activities, there can only be one individual in command. The way in which it was incorporated, attached, or whatever, is not so important. The essence of the theory of resubordination says that once it is there, it is under single command and this commander shall be responsible for its use and its possible misuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I called up page 6 in Serbian and page 8 in English of this same document. We need Article 39 to be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, you can follow this document on your screen as well, although you have a hard copy, I understand. General, we already discussed yesterday the use of Territorial Defence units in discharging the public security duties. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What I would like to emphasise here is that this form of engagement is also decided by the military command, the military hierarchy, and the president; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if we construe the previous provision and this provision together, that is an obvious example of a singleness of authority. We have one commander who is commanding both the police and the Territorial Defence. Is that the pyramid of the singleness of authority that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. General, speaking about this provision, and in order not to revisit it, let's go back to page 2 in the Serbian and page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please zoom in on Article 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Read it through, please, and then I'll put a question to you. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to go back to the Law on All People's Defence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the same law with the same title of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I suppose that you are familiar with the provisions contained therein because we are talking here about the concept of All People's Defence. So you know that within that system all participants within the country were obliged to prepare for the situation of an imminent threat of war or war, and, to that end, to adapt their organisation, draw up wartime plans, establish sort of war staffs of their own that would direct these organs under such circumstances. Are aware with these provisions from these earlier laws?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. And that was implemented in practice. There were even some military exercises and police exercises carried out. Each local commune, municipality, district, and republic were obliged to adhere to these provisions of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This obligation was equally valid for the state organs, including the ministries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior was also obliged to have its own plan of work in the event of an immediate threat of war, or a war, to have proper organisation structure in place, to have its own staff that would be directing this organ, and so on and so forth. That's what the law says; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your report, in paragraph 56, quote the Law on Defence of Republika Srpska, and you are actually listing here the specific obligations of the Ministry of Interior within the context of the preparations for defence. Can you see your paragraph 56?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that from the time when the federal law was in force until the last one that you referred to, this obligation remained continuous and identical; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to show you a document. It's in your tab, I think, 14. And it's Exhibit 1D46. You can look the whole -- at the whole document in tab 14, and, after that, we're going to comment on it. Yes, it's tab 4 -- 14 in our binder.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, this order by the minister of the interior, you will agree with me, that it is an example of the application of the obligation that was defined for the minister in the laws that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In other words, he defines the ways in which the Ministry of Interior is supposed to function in the case of the imminent threat of war or war.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you noticed that the ministry is supposed to split in two parts? One part, which will continue performing their regular duties and tasks related to public order; and another part, which may be used in combat activities if competent military command submits such a request. Have you noticed this split?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The minister here says that usual peacetime laws and regulations should be applied to the first part, the laws and regulations regulating the normal work of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, the second part of the ministry, let's call it the uniformed part, people carrying arms, in paragraphs 7 and 8 of this order, the minister says: Military regulations shall be applied to this part.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You, as an expert, noticed this split of the ministry in some other segments of work as well in these particular circumstances. For example, when you discussed the co-operation between the military organs and the police organs. This co-operation could only exist in relation to the first part of the ministry, the part that continued performing their regular tasks.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, there can be no co-operation with the second part of the ministry, the part that is being used in combat activities. Because this part is now an integral part of the military structure and subordination, so there can be no talk of co-ordination or co-operation. There are only orders that are carried out. Am I correct in saying this?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. If you take a look at paragraph 7 of this order by the minister, you will see in the third subparagraph: [As read] "While participating in combat operations, the units of the ministry shall be subordinated to the command of the armed forces ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention this, let me ask you the following: Is this the essence of the relationship between the military and the police in time of war or imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I'm afraid your question is not precise enough. I cannot understand it. Relationship is a very, very wide term. If we talk about relationship between the military and the police, that's imprecise. I keep emphasizing here that the relation is very clear, and then there is a command relationship in existence only when the police is part of the command structure of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Your answer was not interpreted in a very precise way. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not fully understand your question. And then I repeated what I had already stated. The relations between the military and the police units, when the latter are engaged in combat activities, are clearly defined, and then we can only speak of a command relationship. The police units are, in such a case, subordinated to a military commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When I put the question to you, I had in mind your previous answer, when you said that it is far more important what kind of relations we have once the police arrives -- arrives into the military structure and is resubordinated to the military commander. That is why I wanted to emphasise what I perceived as the essence of the -- their relationship.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. Now I understand what you wanted to ask me in your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the essence of this relation was condensed by you, if I can put it that way, in a paragraph of your report. It's paragraph 217. And I would like you to confirm whether this paragraph talks about the topic that you've just discussed here.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely what I wrote in paragraph 217. The subject matter of our recent discussion, and, indeed, the discussion in the past few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, let me close on this topic. You have been here for quite a number of days here, answering our questions, and I think that now we have the clear picture about the hierarchy, the pyramid and the principle of the singleness of command --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Sorry, can we not have a speech, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the pyramid of the command over the armed forces has only one summit.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Any occurrence of parallel command encroaches on the principle of the singleness of command and subordination, as well as impinging on the system of defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Any parallel command will not be tolerated by the military hierarchy and structure. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So, if, in a zone of responsibility of a corps commander, a well-armed group of, say, volunteers appears, numbering 1- to 200 men, and they take part in combat activities; however, with their own command, with their own tactics and with their own strategy, without respecting the military hierarchy, the military tactics, and the military strategy, what are the powers at the disposal of the corps commander in this particular situation?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander has powers and competencies enabling him to summon the officer commanding over this particular group and to order him that they should all voluntarily be transferred into the hierarchy and under the command of the corps. If they refuse to do this, he has the power and, indeed, the duty to disarm them, to break them apart, and, ultimately, destroy in case that they resist his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, what do you mean by "destroy them"? Would that be to arrest them and incarcerate them? Or do you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if this group puts up an armed resistance against the regular units of the corps, then the regular units have the powers to engage them in combat. I agree with you that the corps commander - and I said that his first option would be the offer of voluntary surrender - and then, of course, he also has the option of arresting them and prosecuting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, there is one thing I would like to know in the end. What is the scope of the competency of military commanders in case of an imminent threat of war? So my question is very direct and very specific: Does this hold true in the whole territory where this particular emergency had been proclaimed? I'm talking here about the powers of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The powers of the commanders pertain to all military officers throughout the territory where the imminent threat of war had been proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my cross-examination is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General Kovacevic, just before I turn to your report and other matters, on that last answer, I just want to make sure we all understand. The powers of a commander in an area where, as you put it, a threat of war has been declared, pertained to military officers. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, we should be more precise here, Ms. Korner, when defining what is military personnel, how we defined this term during the imminent threat of war, if you permit me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I say, I'm going to come onto that, because there is a very clear definition, is there not, of who or what is a member of the military, in the law.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in case of an imminent threat of war, and you can see this from the documents that I analysed, a general public mobilisation is proclaimed. The duty to report to the mobilisation is a duty on all citizens, I think males between 17 and 60 and females between 17 and 55. So they are all military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. But it doesn't apply -- as I say, we're going to look at the definition of who is in the military later. It does not, therefore, apply to those who are in the police unless they have been - and let's use the word "resubordinated" because everybody has been using that - they have been resubordinated into the military, attached to the military.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the police had its reserve force, if that's what you're thinking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear so that we don't have any more discussion or argument about this. Military personnel does not include members of the MUP unless they have been resubordinated to the military. Is there a problem with the question, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lost my thought, Ms. Korner. I didn't follow you carefully enough. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will. From what you have told us, the military -- I'm sorry, let me just get the exact answer. Military -- the powers of commanders, you told Mr. Cvijetic, pertain to all military officers throughout the territory where the imminent threat of war has been complained -- proclaimed. I now repeat the question: All military officers does not include members of the MUP, reserve or fully authorised, unless they have been resubordinated to military command.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Ms. Korner. However, we saw a number of cases when an entire MUP force was resubordinated to military command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. General, I'm not arguing that at all. I just wanted to confirm that's what you were saying, and you've confirmed that's what you were saying. All right. I now would like to ask you about your report in general, and your expertise. I'm just going to get my ... Apart from the written report that you produced for the Popovic and others case, have you ever produced a report before, or since Popovic, and before this one, for the purposes of trial proceedings?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you ever testified before, because you weren't asked that earlier on, in any of the trials either in Serbia, Croatia, or in Bosnia and Herzegovina for war crimes committed during the 1992 to 1995 conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I take it from that this is the first time that you have testified as an expert in any kind of court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you understand -- and I don't mean this in any rude or insulting way. Because it's the first time, do you understand the rules that govern expert testimony?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, when approached by the Defence counsel, I understood my role here to appear as a military expert witness. In this sense, I prepared, wishing to assist the counsel and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand how you came to testify, and I'm going to come back to that one as well. I'm asking you now whether you understand what the duties of an expert witness, or, indeed, an expert in any kind of proceeding, are.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood the words of the Presiding Judge and when I pronounced my solemn obligation, that my duty here was to tell the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I quite understand that, General. But what I'm asking you is you have any idea of what is required of an expert and, in particular, an expert's report. And can you tell us what you understand is the duty of an expert when preparing a report for court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It is an unclear question. Ms. Korner should put a direct question to the expert. What is she seeking to extract? Otherwise the witness will not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... indeed I was going to suggest, Ms. Korner, that the -- the way the question, the open-ended way in which the question is phrased would be difficult even for a lawyer to answer. And since you have the advantage of cross-examining, I would have thought it would be more helpful if you would directly suggest to him what the obligations of an expert are, and go from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that I have the right to the ask leading questions, but I thought, in fairness to the General, I ought to give him a chance before I put to him various matters to see if he can tell us what he understands his duties were before he prepared the report. But I'm perfectly prepared to put the -- the various things to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you understand that it's the duty of an expert to be objective?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I see my duty is that I'm here to tell the truth and that I need to provide an accurate interpretation of military rules and regulations that I refer to in my report. I'm also here to use those rules and regulations, in order to provide an accurate interpretation of the documents put before me by the Court in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me explain to you, then, General, what I mean by "objective." Do you understand that you have to look at the material with an open mind before coming to a conclusion about that material?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, first, you need to tell me what specific material you have in mind and what conclusion of mine may have been one-sided or biased.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Believe you me, General, I'm going to come to all of that. But, at the moment, I'm trying to establish, so that the Court understands and all of us understand, whether you approached the material that you are were asked to deal with by the Defence with an open mind? And let me explain what I mean by "an open mind." That you didn't just look at material for documents or statements which supported what the Defence wanted you to say?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the focus of my report was on military rules, documents, and regulations. I attempted an interpretation of those rules and regulations which I also relied on in order to interpret the documents provided by Defence in the course of the past few days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, General, we'll see in a moment that that's not right, that your report doesn't just deal with military documents, rules, and regulations. So I will repeat for the last time the question I asked. Do you understand that as an expert it is your duty to look at documents with a -- and rules and regulations, with an open mind?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Do you understand that an expert report should also include matters which do not support the -- the theory or the side which you are trying to advance?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I used the documents, rules and regulations that I could gain access to, and this is what I based my report on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll come onto, then, what you were given access to in a moment. In writing a report, do you understand the importance of giving source -- sources for the -- the matters that you put into the report? Certainly matters of fact.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what's the reason for that? Why is that important?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used some general written material that can be found in the attachment to my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I -- I'm coming on to -- I will come onto the specifics. But I'm asking you now: Why it is important - you say you know it's important - to give sources. Why is that important?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume it is important in order to tell the truth, and I undertook that obligation as an expert before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me put it to you as I -- do you understand that it's important so that what you say, based on a source, can be checked by anybody who is reading the report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that an original source is better than a secondary source? And I'll explain what I mean by that. In other words, that the original document, or the original account, is better than a secondary source who has put it into a book or reporting on it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends, Ms. Korner, on the context and topic. I wouldn't necessarily ascribe advantage to either one or the other. I'm not sure what you have in mind specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't it be better to look at the original of a military order rather than somebody describing that military order in a book?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. If the original is accessible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously if it is not accessible, I accept. Now, do you understand the importance of accurate quotes? If you're quoting from a document or from a book that it should be quoted accurately.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I ask you about your methodology in preparing this report. You set it out at page -- just a moment. Let me just find it. Yep. Well, I don't think ... just a moment, Your Honours, I'm sorry. I was going to say that the methodology isn't ... Yes, notes on methodology. Page 5 in the English. The report is 0031D2. I have no idea, I am afraid, what it is in the B/C/S, so I'm going to have to rely on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Same page, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph is better to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. You're quite right. Yes, paragraph 11. It's page 5 in each, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now you say in paragraph 11 after you describe what your approach was to analyse and synthesise documents. "The basic method I used was analyse and synthesis." Can you just explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a well-known method used in the production of many a report, even scientific papers. One analyses the contents of certain documents, rules, and regulations. The crux of the matter is the contents, based on which, one can make conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand analyse. What does analyse and synthesise mean. What do you mean by synthesise?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the result of a thinking process. One analyses documents and draws conclusions. By using specific parts, you make a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So what synthesise means is your analysing the documents and drawing conclusions from them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if the conclusion was contrary when you'd analysed these documents to the -- what you'd been asked to show, would you put that into the report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I came across such a instance, I would have to specify it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to move from the general to the specific. When were you first asked to compile a report on behalf of Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I mentioned that yesterday. It is a fact that I had very little time to prepare this report. I think I was approached in late February or early March of this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Really? Well, presumably you have an exact note of the date. Could you tell us, please, the exact note of the date.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the date is the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask what you're referring to there, General. General, the piece of paper you've just put back into your brief-case. You can take it out again. Can I ask you what it is, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an overview of the time flow. It was forwarded to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's confidential. It's a time sheet for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That may be so, but I'm going to ask to see it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because it is correspondence between Registry and with the expert. It is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's relevant. It's not privileged. And I'm going to ask Your Honours to allow me to have a look at it because the amount of time that the General spent working on this report, and actually in his own interest, is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This matter is a little more complex than first appears. We would return to it. Could you continue --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no problem in showing this. But since this touches upon a sensitive relationship between OLAD and the expert, I believe it should be done in consultation with the Registry to see whether this should be published publicly. As for the contents, we have no objection to having it shown to Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the Registry, in terms of that separate question, that is something that the Registry is going to inquire into and advise the Chamber accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, this should be checked; and if it is not a problem, Mr. Kovacevic will provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, by whom were you asked to do the report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By Mr. Dragan Krgovic, Defence Attorney.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that request in writing or verbally?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a verbal request, as far as I recall. I knew him from earlier times. As I have said, we worked on a previous case together.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that; the Popovic case. What were the terms of reference? What were you actually asked to do a report on? And, again, did you get those terms of reference in writing?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be honest: We discussed in his office for a few hours. That was the first time round. I hesitated to accept the task because the police is an institution I'm not familiar with, or to be more precise, I'm less privy to its working than the military institutions are. However, in conversation with Mr. Krgovic, I realized that the topic of my report was to be the use of the police in combat activities. That is why I accepted. In order for it to be explained, such use of civilian police in combat, we need to view it through military terms, military documents and military rules. The terms include military command, resubordination, coordinated action, and attachment. Once I realized that, I accepted to draft a report of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, General, thank you for telling us. As you said - and it's not a criticism of you at all - you are not in any sense an expert in police matters, are you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Except when the police is used in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'll come back to that one. You've never studied, have you, the interaction between police and military from the point of view of the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've never looked at the documents about the police use by the military from the police side. The documents that the police issue. And I don't just mean for 1992 -- for 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my CV, Ms. Korner, I stated that the focus of my work was education and training of members of the unit of which I was part of. I educated and trained those members, but in order to be able to do that, I had to read a huge number of books, cover various areas of expertise, and read documents. For example, each new regulation, when it is published that pertains to the army, I have to take it to the unit and to brief my unit about this particular regulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I had an opportunity to encounter various contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I'm sorry, General. I think you didn't understand the question. Have you ever looked at documents produced by the MUP before the conflict when there was a federal state, or states of Yugoslavia, or during the conflict of the police, apart from what you've been shown by Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had an opportunity to see them earlier in practice, not to a large extent though. There was some sort of co-operation with MUP units, and there were some contacts between the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to spend more time than that. You had a conversation of some hours with Mr. Krgovic. Did you make notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is it a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I have a question of Mr. Krgovic before we rise. So perhaps the witness can be escorted out of the courtroom a little ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krgovic, this comes back to the question the Chamber has indicated that it would deal with, Ms. Korner's application and your objection. Did I understand you correctly to say that you would have no objection to the document in question being shown to the Prosecutor without it being -- coming into evidence as a public document? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the list of hours that the witness has to account for to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the problem we see here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I know what it is. But my precise question is -- and I appreciate the matter of it not being made an item of evidence. My only question is whether I understood you correctly when I thought you had said that you had no difficulty with counsel for the opposite side seeing it and leaving it at that without -- the question of it being a matter of evidence not arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to see it but not to ask any questions about it or use this document for whatever purposes that might arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of course, I don't have to see the document. It was merely to short-circuit things. I could simply ask the General to tell us each day that he worked on this report, and that wouldn't be objectionable. But it would waste an awful lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I just wanted to clarify --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- because you said you would return to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I will be asking questions on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you know what the problem is? In principle, this is inequality of arms of parties in the proceedings. If you ask somebody to prepare a report and that is what the Prosecution was doing with the people who were working for them, in that case, they didn't have to record the number of the hours. However, when we engage an outside expert we to have the -- know -- the number of hours, and we have to ask him or her about how many hours he spent because we have no other available records. And this is this principle of inequality and the inferior position of the Defence with respect to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to do with inequality of arms. It's to do with how much time the expert had to do the report and look at the documents, which is a relevant issue and is something, as I say, in fairness to him. If he had a limited amount of time, that may explain a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then put a simple question to him. Ask him quite simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, why don't you just ask: How many hours did you work on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can. But I'm anxious to see exactly how many hours he worked on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, we'll take the break and come back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just briefly address the Bench with regard to the last topic that Ms. Korner and I discussed. During the break, I received information that the document that the witness has with him is basically my document. In other words, that's a translation of the summary of his report that I was supposed to submit to the Registry but somehow he has retained this copy. In it, it is roughly stated how many hours were used, which -- and that report was supposed to be submitted to the Registry. So basically that's my document. Pursuant to Rule 70(A) which reads that reports, memoranda and other internal documents that are connected with the investigation or preparation of the case and have been drafted by any of the party, its associates or assistants are not subject to disclosure or notice in line with the provisions of the said Rule. So we have a crystal-clear situation here, Your Honours, that is our internal document that shouldn't be disclosed or publicised for any purposes whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just know what -- would Your Honours be kind enough to establish how Mr. Krgovic received the information over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Informed by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. The -- during the break, the Chamber requested the Registry to have sight of the document that the witness had, and the Registry was the means of communication with Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. Well, Your Honours, I don't want to waste time on pursuing the matter. I'm not sure it is as clear-cut that this is a privileged document. But nonetheless, if it is a privileged document, it's been waived by being supplied to the witness, is not, in any sense, part of the team investigating. But I don't think it is necessary to waste any more time on this. So perhaps we can carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we have the witness back on the stand and we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I should point that the first communication of the Court Officer would have had counsel. Counsel hasn't seen the document; so it's been an oral communication between the Registry and counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, I want to go back to look at the document you looked at for when you were first instructed. Do we understand this, that this is a document that contains your hours and a summary of your potential evidence prepared by Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. The document is in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. General, can I ask you, then, please, can you tell us, did you keep your own record of the time you spent compiling this report, in order to submit it to Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't keep any special record of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, how did you -- how did you -- or well, I should ask you this first. Did you give Mr. Krgovic any note of the hours you spent preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't give him any written notes. I just informed him orally, off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, General, wasn't it made clear to you that the time you spent and which you supplied was the basis on which the Registry would pay you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were aware of that. Well, didn't you think it important, therefore, to keep an accurate record of the time that you spent working on this report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had this all -- all this information, Ms. Korner, in my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Really. All right. Can you tell us, then, please, General, between the 1st of March -- well, firstly, when did you submit the report to Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, did you submit the report by post or by e-mail?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the report personally to Mr. Krgovic at his law office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When was that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I believe that it happened about a month after I had worked on drafting the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's have a look. You can use the document that you were provided with. You told us that you were first instructed on the 1st of March. When is the last day, according to the document that you have in your possession, that you worked on the report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 31st of March, all right. And that's the date you say you took it to Mr. Krgovic in his office, is it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that that was precisely the date, but I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see -- are you sure this is an accurate record, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, your report was filed with this Court on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was towards the end of March. I may have been mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What does it say on the document? You've given us the 31st of March. You said -- I asked you what -- when is the last day, according to the document you have in your possession, you worked on the report. You said the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's a difference between the last day that he worked on it, and the day he filed it. Because there were other problems in the intervening period. So what is recorded there has nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, what -- your question was what does it say on the document you've given us, what document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] the one he had in his possession, which is Mr. Krgovic's document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The one you would not pursue questioning about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, because I got the distinct impression I was not being encouraged to pursue questioning about, but I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That is what you are doing. Are you pursuing on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I'm trying to get -- Sorry, Your Honours. I'm trying to get the dates when he worked on the report. And all he can tell us is that what's on that document. I'm sorry, Your Honours, I didn't appreciate ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, are you saying that after you'd handed the report to Mr. Krgovic, you did some further work?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there were some technical problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what technical problems?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with regard to footnotes and other technical problems that I'm not good at solving, so I consulted the people from Mr. Krgovic's office, and after I had handed in the documents, we continued touching it up in view of making preparations for my appearance here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So do I understand that the report that was filed, which we have copies of, there are other versions of it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there are no other versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you produced the final report that was filed, did you send a draft to Mr. Krgovic or anybody else on his team?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't send it to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations, with Mr. Krgovic or anybody else on his team before you produced the version that was filed, about the report.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I finished my report, I talked to some professors from the Military Academy about some of the topics that I covered in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also talked to a number of generals and military officers who had been in the VRS throughout the whole period. But that was all in order to verify my views, my conclusions, and for better preparation for this trial. Better preparation of me personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's leave it aside, preparation for the trial. Did you talk to these generals before you gave the final version of this report to Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He already answered on that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you talk to those generals before you prepared the final version of this report.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I first drafted the report by myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no. You did a draft of the report - is this right? - then you spoke to the generals, and then you did your final version; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's misleading. It's completely misleading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, just so that we all understand: Did you speak to the generals before you submitted the report to Mr. Krgovic and after you had done a draft?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked to those people, I only verified my views, and I made preparations for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, it's not an answer to the question. Was the talking to the other generals, when you had done a draft but before you gave Mr. Krgovic the final version, or after you had delivered the final version?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having delivered the final version to Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you -- I'll go back to my original question. Did you speak to Mr. Krgovic or any member of the Defence team before you delivered your final version about the contents of your report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Mr. Krgovic on a number of occasions while I was working on the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did you tell him what you were going to put into the report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you make any changes to what you were going to put into the report, as a result of your conversations with Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more of a consultation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't quite understand what that means. What do you mean by "a consultation"?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wouldn't bring him a document so that he could put in some corrections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But I want to know what you mean by "consultations."

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I had a dilemma. Then I would ask him, he would give me a reply. I would memorize it. I will go home. I would sit behind my computer, and I would put it into the report that I was currently working on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Give us an example of a dilemma in which Mr. Krgovic gave you the answer.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember with any precision right now. I'm merely answering your questions. And I'm explaining the methods that I used in my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. When I started asking you questions this morning, I asked you if you understood the duties of an expert. Did you understand that you should have said in the report who had assisted you with the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the existence of this obligation. But I emphasise once again: That I drafted the report on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, General, I understand that you did the physical drafting of it on your own. But from what you just told us, it contained input from Mr. Krgovic who solved your dilemma.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, or to be more precise, it was really a suggestion. Or I shouldn't really say "suggestion." In those cases when I had small problems in interpretation of certain laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do you mean he gave you the interpretation, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He helped me. He helped me to resolve a dilemma. Legal dilemma.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, General, did -- did you understand that, to the reader of this report, this all looks like your own work, your own conclusions, based on, as you put it, your own analysis and synthesis?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, in actual fact, the reality is that it isn't, isn't it? It contains parts that you got from Mr. Krgovic who solved your dilemmas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such thing in this report. The dilemmas were only inside my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, firstly, let's go back to these dilemmas then. How many times, if you can recall, did you consult Mr. Krgovic about a dilemma that was in your head?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You've told us you memorialised what he said and then went back and put it in your report. Why didn't you write it down at the time, rather than trying to remember what he told you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in the middle of my career, I lost half of one of my fingers, and then, during the remainder of my career, it made it difficult for me to use my right hand for writing. All my speeches, public speeches, speeches on television, all my lectures I did ex cathedra. I was well known in the public as an officer with this practice. I never had a single piece of paper in front of me at the time, and even now I have trouble dealing with the papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, is that -- your explanation is that you can't write. So do I understand that you actually didn't type this report?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can use computer. I can type on a computer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you can't write with --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can write, but I hate it. I have difficulties in writing, and I have no need to write.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But rather than trying to remember what Mr. Krgovic was telling you, wouldn't it have been better to have taken, even if it was a bit of trouble, the time to write it down?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it would have been a better idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there any way of identifying in your report which are the parts on which you got the answer to your dilemma from Mr. Krgovic, as you tell us you can't remember what the dilemmas were?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go through the entire report, in order to find those instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you to do that, General, with the leave of the Court, right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may be that an adjournment would be required so that the General can sit there and do it. But I think this is important enough to be dealt with before we go any further because it seems to me that, at the moment, there is a submission that I'm going to be making to Your Honours about this whole report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I hear your application, Ms. Korner, but is -- can't you move on to another area and then come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. Because -- if the answer is I anticipate that the application will be that we're not going any further with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think -- if Mr. Krgovic wants to address you on this, then the witness ought to leave court in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Rather than hearing what Mr. Krgovic has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Fine. But before he does that, I have a question to ask the witness. General Kovacevic, I don't know whether you understood Ms. Korner's application but how long would it take you to go through the report to isolate the passages that are of concern to her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is going to be very difficult for me. Because those details are, in my opinion, very irrelevant. Otherwise I would be able to remember all those instances right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... wrongly translated. It must be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. On the transcript it says "irrelevant" I heard "relevant".

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I heard very relevant. I don't think that is what he said - sorry, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, could you repeat your answer again, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to the Presiding Judge that this was going to be very difficult for me to remember the details, the legal details, because they were less important. If I cannot remember them right now on the spot they must have been less important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, let's explore a little more. You say the legal details. Can you identify what details you're talking about? Are you talking about your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object on this line of question because it is completely misleading the evidence. The witness first said nothing of this dilemma is part of his report. And now, Ms. Korner, trying to push, to mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can the witness leave court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he speaks some English so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: General Kovacevic, the usher will escort you from court to the holding area briefly then we will tell you -- we would inform you as to where we go from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is what I want to say. The witness clearly answered the question posed by Ms. Korner that not a single dilemma was part of the report. And yet Ms. Korner is pressing onto the witness and asking him to show these particular parts. The witness is unable to remember which parts they are because he says that they're not important. To exert pressure on the witness to request him to read through the whole report in order to remember those details is really unnecessary because none of the details are in the report. So Ms. Korner is only confusing the witness with this request. This is my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I fully understand --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I fully understand what you're saying Mr. Krgovic. But the nature of these proceedings are such that it seems to me that opposing counsel is right to press this issue, because what we are left with on the state of the evidence at this point is that the report which has been put into evidence and which is a part of the case for your client was, in part, and it may very well be that at the end of the day you're perfectly correct that such assistance as you gave were totally inconsequential and of no moment in terms of the final work product. But the -- certainly counsel is entitled to explore the -- to the extent that she can, the -- how -- how much this assistance, to use as vague a term as possible may have influenced the result, and to that extent the witness would have to be allowed some time to go through this and answer it, if he is able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... point draw Mr. Krgovic's attention to the exact question and answer I asked. He -- I suppose I ought to go back ... oh, sorry, Your Honours, a little bit further. I asked at line 19 of page 35: [As read] "Did you speak to Mr. Krgovic or any member of the Defence team before you delivered your final version about the contents of your report? "A. I spoke to Mr. Krgovic on a number of occasions while I was working on the report. "Q. Did you tell him what you were going to put into the report? "A. Yes. "Q. Did you make any changes to what you were going to put into the report as a result of your conversations with Mr. Krgovic? "A. It was more of a consultation. "Q. I don't understand what that means. What do you mean by a consultation? "A. Ms. Korner, I wouldn't bring him a document so he could put in some corrections. "Q. No. But I want to know what you mean by consultations. "A. Sometimes I had a dilemma." This is the part. "Then I would ask him, he would give me a reply. I would memorize it. I will go home." I think it must be I would go home. "I would sit behind a computer and I would put it into the report that I was currently working on. "Q. Give us an example of a dilemma in which Mr. Krgovic gave you the answer. "A. I can't remember with any precision now. I'm merely answering your questions and I'm explaining the methods." Then I asked him about the duty to say who had assisted with his report. Question at 37, line 2: [As read] "Q. I understand that you did the physical drafting of it on your own but from what you just told us, it contained input from Mr. Krgovic who solved your dilemma. "A. More often, or to be more precise. It was really a suggestion or I shouldn't say suggestion. In those cases when I had small problems in interpretation of certain laws and regulations. "Q. I'm sorry. Do you mean he gave you the interpretation, General. "A. He helped me. He helped me to resolve a dilemma, legal dilemmas." Then, in actual fact -- there was a bit about understanding for the reader you had to know who had done it. "In actual fact the reality is, isn't it, that it contains parts that you got from Mr. Krgovic who solved your dilemmas; is that right? "There's no such thing in this report. The dilemmas were only inside our head -- my head." Then going back to the dilemma, he said three or four times. And then we had this explanation about his hand and then identifying the parts. Now, Your Honour, I may as well deal with this right now while the witness is out of court on why I've asked this. If, as I anticipate and he has more or less said he can't give, cannot identify the parts that he got from Mr. Krgovic, and Mr. Krgovic cannot give evidence about this matter, it's one of the problems, I suppose, of direct contact between counsel and a witness. Unless he is going to leave the case and become a witness. The general says he cannot identify either what the actual dilemma was other than it was to do with interpretation or which parts of the report. Your Honours, the one thing about an expert report in order - and it's not, of course, in evidence yet it is merely proposed, awaiting the result of cross-examination - is that it should be the report and conclusions of the person giving evidence. If someone else has assisted him, then he should make it clear in what areas and in what aspects. And Your Honours it would be my application if that is the case, that he is unable to do this, that in fact that all his evidence and, indeed, his report are, as it were, null and void, as it were. And had we known this earlier, if Mr. Krgovic had established that with the witness, how he prepared the report, we probably wouldn't have gone much further. But that would be my application. But one way or another, in any event, Your Honours may feel it's important that he identify where he was given assistance by Mr. Krgovic. Particularly in a report and evidence that purports to support in some respects, not all, the Defence case about resubordination and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in reply to the request by Ms. Korner, I can only say that the application mentioned should be left for the end of the cross-examination and my additional examination of this witness. And then, having heard everything from this witness about his methods, she should maybe then proceed. But, however, the gist of my objection is as follows: Ms. Korner does not have the right to continue the cross-examination of the witness but if she does that, she should do it in a proper manner. Take, for example, the last paragraph read out. The one in which the witness clearly stated that not a single dilemma found its way into the report. Now, to ask the witness to find the dilemmas in the report after having received such a reply is improper. That's the gist of my objection. The witness clearly stated that none of the dilemmas are part of the report. So he cannot be requested to look for something that doesn't exist. That is why I think that Ms. Korner is confusing the witness. She is requesting him to find something that does not exist in the report. In any case, in relation to the application by Ms. Korner, I respectfully request the Chamber to decide on the application only after the cross-examination and re-direct examination have been finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] in fact, the witness is -- has given on the face of it what appears to be slightly contradictory answers but the first answer is clear: He spoke to Mr. Krgovic; he went home; and he put it into his report. Your Honours, my application at the moment that he be given the time to go through that report and see if he can identify any dilemmas that he received assistance on from Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise and come back with a ruling on this application at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm terribly sorry to interrupt you. I was just wondering over the break, I don't know if the Trial Chamber feels it's appropriate that -- that the Defence of Stanisic is also heard on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Pardon our oversight, Mr. Zecevic. By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, on what basis? This is -- it's a separate case. This is the witness not for Mr. Stanisic but for Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's the locus for Mr. Zecevic to address you on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let me hear what he has to say and remember the Stanisic team did cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honours. As a matter of fact, I would like to first explain to Ms. Korner. We cross-examined this witness and therefore we cross-examined the witnesses for the Prosecutor we're entitled to rely on their answers. Not only that, but we can rely on the parts of the expert report even from the OTP witnesses. That is the connection. Now, Your Honours, the -- we understand that the position so far from -- throughout this trial was that the Trial Chamber will decide on the admissibility of the expert report at the end of the -- of the cross and the re-examination of -- of the expert witness. It was the practice that we had since the very beginning. And the expert witnesses for the Prosecution, the Stanisic Defence, and I think the -- the situation should continue and it will be only logical that it does in this case as well. From -- as a practical matter, Your Honours, there is -- for Ms. Korner, there is always a possibility that during the cross-examination which I'm -- I think she will conduct, that when she comes to a certain conclusion that she wants to challenge, she can always ask the witness whether this particular conclusion was raised, for example, with Mr. Krgovic or any other person and whether that was the dilemma that was discussed between them. And then we would be able, or you, actually, Your Honours would be able to assess the -- the expert report in all -- with the totality of the evidence concerning that. And that is why we believe that -- we join the submission by Mr. Krgovic, that the decision on the admissibility of this report be -- be taken at the end of the -- of the cross and re-examination of this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate it, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you, yourself, said it I appreciated that what -- that your -- that you are praying in aid the point that Mr. Krgovic made. Could the usher please escort the witness in. And while the witness is on his way in, Ms. Korner, could you refer to page 38, lines 18 to 22 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, did Your Honour say 28 to 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 38, lines 18 to 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where he says, I would have to go through the entire report to find the instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's the answer. The question that precedes it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Is there any way in identifying in your report which are the ..." [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is going to invite you to put that question again, but let's have the witness return to the stand first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: General Kovacevic, from time to time, in the course of trials, these procedural issues have to be resolved and that is why you were stood down while we heard from counsel on this matter. The course that the Chamber has decided upon is that we will take an early adjournment today and have you continue tomorrow morning at the usual time that we resume, at 9.00, but the -- overnight, the question which counsel would have put to you and which we will now invite her to put again so that you remember it, is something that we would ask you to reflect upon, and then we will, as I said, continue with your answer tomorrow morning. Could you put the question again, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, is there any way for you to identify in your report which are the parts on which you got the answer to your dilemma from Mr. Krgovic? And full question was: As you tell us you can't remember what the dilemmas were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, as I said, you would think about counsel's question and we would hear your answer when we resume tomorrow. So unless there is anything else, we take the adjournment to 9.00, and I believe we are still in this courtroom tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We think we're back in III, Your Honours, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In Courtroom III. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
